prog-bbm-001.question: In a Boston Scientific dual-chamber pacemaker, what is the principle of the RYTHMIQ algorithm?
options: AAI(R) with slower VVI backup, switching to DDD(R) if AV synchrony is lost
AAI(R) with V backup on the next cycle, DDD(R) if 2 of 4 A-A cycles lack an R
DDD(R) with a periodically extended AV delay to search for intrinsic conduction
ADI(R) while conduction persists, DDD(R) if 3 of 8 cycles lack conduction
commentaires: Correct: RYTHMIQ operates in AAI(R) with a slower VVI backup running in the background and switches to DDD(R) if AV synchrony is lost.
Incorrect: ventricular backup on the next cycle and the 2-of-4 criterion belong to Medtronic MVP.
Incorrect: periodic AV delay extension while remaining in DDD is AV Search+ (or Abbott VIP), not RYTHMIQ itself.
Incorrect: ADI(R) with a return to DDD(R) after 3 of 8 cycles without conduction is Biotronik Vp Suppression.
prog-bbm-001.explication: RYTHMIQ is an algorithm designed to minimise unnecessary ventricular pacing in patients with preserved AV conduction. The device operates in AAI(R) while a VVI backup mode runs in the background at a rate below the lower rate limit: as long as conduction is intact, the ventricle is not paced. If loss of AV synchrony is detected, the device switches to DDD(R), then returns to AAI(R) once conduction resumes. Unlike Medtronic MVP, RYTHMIQ does not need to "drop" QRS complexes to switch to DDD(R). It is only available when the permanent programmed mode is DDD(R). It must not be confused with AV Search+ (AV delay hysteresis, on which it relies to return to AAI(R)) or with Biotronik Vp Suppression (DDD(R) ↔ ADI(R) switching).
prog-bbm-001.aRetenir: RYTHMIQ = AAI(R) with a reduced-rate VVI backup, switching to DDD(R) if AV synchrony is lost.

prog-bbm-002.question: A Boston Scientific pacemaker is programmed DDD with RYTHMIQ on. At what rate does the backup VVI pacing run during the AAI phase if the lower rate limit (LRL) is 60 bpm? And if it is 40 bpm?
prog-bbm-002.reponseAttendue: The VVI backup runs 15 bpm below the LRL, bounded between 30 and 60 bpm: 45 bpm for an LRL of 60; 30 bpm (not 25) for an LRL of 40.
prog-bbm-002.explication: During the AAI(R) phase of RYTHMIQ, the Boston Scientific manual states that backup VVI pacing is delivered 15 bpm below the LRL. This backup rate is bounded: never below 30 bpm and never above 60 bpm. With an LRL of 60, the backup rate is therefore 45 bpm; with an LRL of 40, the raw calculation would give 25, but the lower bound imposes 30 bpm. As long as conduction is present, this VVI mode does not intervene. In practice, this explains why isolated slow ventricular cycles may be seen on a Holter before the switch to DDD(R).
prog-bbm-002.aRetenir: RYTHMIQ VVI backup = LRL − 15 bpm, bounded between 30 and 60 bpm.

prog-bbm-003.question: During the AAI(R) phase of RYTHMIQ, which criterion switches the pacemaker to DDD(R)?
options: Two consecutive blocked P waves with no ventricular event
Six consecutive PR intervals longer than the programmed maximum
3 slow ventricular beats within a window of 11 beats
No ventricular sensed event in 2 of the last 4 A-A cycles
commentaires: Incorrect: 2 consecutive blocked P waves is the complete AV block criterion of MicroPort SafeR.
Incorrect: 6 consecutive excessively long PR intervals is the first-degree AV block criterion of MicroPort SafeR.
Correct: RYTHMIQ switches to DDD(R) when 3 slow beats (at least 150 ms late) occur out of 11.
Incorrect: absence of ventricular sensing in 2 of 4 A-A cycles is the Medtronic MVP criterion.
prog-bbm-003.explication: RYTHMIQ monitors for loss of AV synchrony by counting slow ventricular beats. A slow beat is a ventricular event, sensed or paced, occurring at least 150 ms later than the AAI(R) pacing interval. When 3 slow beats occur within a window of 11 beats, the device switches to DDD(R) and stores a RYTHMIQ episode with 20 s of EGM. The criteria "2 consecutive blocked P waves" and "6 long PR intervals" belong to MicroPort SafeR, and the "2 of 4 A-A cycles without ventricular sensing" criterion to Medtronic MVP. Mixing up manufacturers in this way is a common pitfall in the device clinic.
prog-bbm-003.aRetenir: RYTHMIQ switches to DDD(R) after 3 slow ventricular beats out of 11.

prog-bbm-004.question: In a Boston Scientific patient with RYTHMIQ on, if AV Search+ is programmed Off, a switch from AAI(R) to DDD(R) occurs only once: the device then remains in DDD(R) until it is reprogrammed.
options: True
False
commentaires: Correct: without AV Search+, nothing tests for recovery of conduction, so after the first switch the device remains in DDD(R).
Incorrect: RYTHMIQ's return to AAI(R) depends on AV Search+; turning it off makes DDD(R) permanent after the first episode.
prog-bbm-004.explication: The return from DDD(R) to AAI(R) with VVI backup relies on AV Search+: if AV Search+ remains in AV hysteresis for at least 25 cycles and fewer than 2 of the last 10 cycles are V-paced, the device returns to AAI(R). Without AV Search+, no mechanism tests for recovery of conduction, so the pacemaker stays in DDD(R). The Boston Scientific manual even presents this as a deliberate option when the switch is intended to occur only once. This is a classic pitfall: turning AV Search+ off "to keep things simple" effectively disables RV pacing reduction after the first episode.
prog-bbm-004.aRetenir: RYTHMIQ's return to AAI(R) depends on AV Search+; without it, DDD(R) becomes permanent.

prog-bbm-005.question: Regarding the AV Search+ algorithm in Boston Scientific pacemakers, which statements are correct?
options: It periodically extends the AV delay (Search AV Delay) for up to 8 cycles to search for intrinsic conduction
It reverts to the programmed AV delay when 2 ventricular paced events occur within a sliding window of 10 cycles
It switches the device to ADI(R) mode as long as intrinsic AV conduction is present
It enforces systematic ventricular pacing during exercise
commentaires: Correct: the Search AV Delay is applied periodically for up to 8 cycles to allow an intrinsic QRS to emerge.
Correct: 2 ventricular paced events within a 10-cycle window trigger a return to the programmed AV delay.
Incorrect: AV Search+ remains in DDD with an extended AV delay; switching to ADI(R) is the principle of Biotronik Vp Suppression.
Incorrect: nothing in AV Search+ enforces ventricular pacing during exercise.
prog-bbm-005.explication: AV Search+ promotes intrinsic AV conduction by allowing an AV delay longer than the programmed one. Periodically (Search Interval), the AV delay is extended for up to 8 cycles; as long as the intrinsic PR intervals remain shorter than the Search AV Delay, hysteresis is maintained. The device reverts to the programmed AV delay if the search finds no intrinsic ventricular activity within 8 cycles, or if 2 ventricular paced events occur within a 10-cycle window. The device stays in DDD: switching to an ADI(R) mode is the principle of Biotronik Vp Suppression. The Search AV Delay must be longer than the maximum paced AV delay, and the programmer does not take it into account when calculating the TARP: if conduction is lost, Wenckebach-type behaviour may appear below the maximum tracking rate.
prog-bbm-005.aRetenir: AV Search+ = AV delay hysteresis that searches for intrinsic conduction and reverts to the programmed delay if the ventricle is paced 2 times in 10 cycles.

prog-bbm-006.question: How does PaceSafe RVAC (Right Ventricular Automatic Capture) work in a Boston Scientific pacemaker?
options: Threshold measured and trended, without ever changing the programmed amplitude
Threshold measured periodically, amplitude at twice threshold, no beat-to-beat check
Threshold measured using AV conduction or sinus rhythm reset
Daily threshold + 0.5 V, capture confirmed on every beat, backup pulse
commentaires: Incorrect: measuring and trending the threshold without adapting the amplitude is the ATM mode of Biotronik Capture Control.
Incorrect: an amplitude at twice threshold without beat-to-beat verification corresponds to Boston Scientific atrial RAAT, not RVAC.
Incorrect: AV conduction and sinus rhythm reset are the atrial methods of Medtronic (Atrial Capture Management).
Correct: RVAC sets the amplitude 0.5 V above the daily threshold, confirms capture on every beat and delivers a backup pulse.
prog-bbm-006.explication: PaceSafe RVAC measures the ventricular threshold every day and sets the amplitude 0.5 V above that threshold (range 0.7 to 3.5 V, pulse width fixed at 0.4 ms). It then confirms capture beat by beat using the evoked response. If loss of capture occurs, a backup pulse of at least 3.5 V is delivered about 70 ms after the primary pulse. If loss of capture is confirmed (2 cycles out of 4), the algorithm is suspended and a new test is performed an hour later. The atrium follows a different logic (RAAT: twice the threshold, without beat-to-beat verification). Threshold monitoring without amplitude adaptation corresponds to Biotronik ATM mode.
prog-bbm-006.aRetenir: RVAC = daily threshold + 0.5 V, capture confirmed on every beat, and a backup pulse if capture is lost.

prog-bbm-007.question: What is the minute ventilation (MV) sensor used for rate response by Boston Scientific based on?
options: Endocardial acceleration measured at the tip of a dedicated lead
Transthoracic impedance, giving respiratory rate and tidal volume
Intracardiac ventricular impedance, reflecting myocardial contractility
An accelerometer measuring vibrations related to physical activity
commentaires: Incorrect: endocardial acceleration measured by a dedicated lead is the MicroPort SonR sensor, used to optimise CRT.
Correct: the MV sensor measures transthoracic impedance; minute ventilation = respiratory rate × tidal volume.
Incorrect: intracardiac impedance, reflecting contractility, is the principle of Biotronik Closed Loop Stimulation.
Incorrect: the accelerometer is a separate, motion-sensitive sensor that can be combined with the MV sensor.
prog-bbm-007.explication: The MV sensor (also called the respiratory sensor) delivers small current pulses and measures transthoracic impedance, which varies with respiration. Minute ventilation, the product of respiratory rate and tidal volume, is used to increase the pacing rate according to physiological demand. The same measurements feed trends such as respiratory rate. The accelerometer is a separate, motion-sensitive sensor that can be combined with MV. Intracardiac ventricular impedance is the signal used by Biotronik Closed Loop Stimulation, and endocardial acceleration that of MicroPort SonR.
prog-bbm-007.aRetenir: MV sensor = transthoracic impedance → respiratory rate × tidal volume.

prog-bbm-008.question: A patient with a Boston Scientific pacemaker with minute ventilation rate response (MV On) is intubated in intensive care. The nurse notes pacing close to the maximum sensor rate with no clinical explanation. What is the appropriate management?
options: Turn off the accelerometer while leaving minute ventilation active
Increase the maximum sensor rate to avoid rate capping
Program the MV sensor Off during mechanical ventilation
Reduce ventricular sensitivity to avoid myopotential oversensing
commentaires: Incorrect: it is the MV sensor, fooled by the ventilator, that is driving the rate; turning off the accelerometer alone changes nothing.
Incorrect: raising the maximum rate would worsen the paced tachycardia without addressing the cause.
Correct: the manual requires the MV sensor to be programmed Off during mechanical ventilation; failing that, a magnet provides asynchronous pacing without rate response.
Incorrect: ventricular sensitivity has nothing to do with the MV sensor; there is no oversensing here.
prog-bbm-008.explication: The Boston Scientific manual states that the MV/respiratory sensor must be programmed Off during mechanical ventilation, otherwise inappropriate sensor-driven rates and misleading respiratory trends may occur. External monitors that inject current (respiratory monitoring, some ECG or haemodynamic monitors) can also distort the impedance measurement and drive the rate up to the maximum sensor rate. If no programmer is available, a magnet provides temporary asynchronous pacing without rate response, provided the magnet response is programmed to asynchronous pacing (Pace Async, the usual setting); the magnet rate then depends on battery status (100 bpm at beginning of life). Turning off only the accelerometer leaves the cause in place, increasing the maximum rate would worsen the problem, and ventricular sensitivity has nothing to do with the sensor.
prog-bbm-008.aRetenir: Mechanical ventilation or impedance-based monitoring: MV sensor Off.

prog-bbm-009.question: What is the purpose of the Rate Smoothing feature in a Boston Scientific pacemaker?
options: Limiting pacing interval changes to a percentage of the last R-R interval
Pacing at a high rate for a programmed period after a sudden drop in rate
Lowering the lower rate during programmed sleep hours
Shortening the escape interval after an ectopic beat to eliminate the pause
commentaires: Correct: Rate Smoothing limits cycle-to-cycle change to 3–25% of the last R-R interval, both upwards and downwards.
Incorrect: this is the principle of Sudden Brady Response (or Medtronic Rate Drop Response), which is incompatible with Rate Smoothing On.
Incorrect: a programmed night-time reduction in rate corresponds to a Sleep-type function, not Rate Smoothing.
Incorrect: eliminating the post-ectopic pause is the principle of Medtronic Rate Stabilization.
prog-bbm-009.explication: Rate Smoothing limits abrupt changes in pacing rate. The allowed change is a percentage of the last R-R interval (3–25% in 3% steps), programmable separately for increases (Rate Smoothing Up) and decreases (Rate Smoothing Down). The feature is useful at the onset and termination of a tracked atrial arrhythmia, in addition to mode switching (ATR): it prevents abrupt rises in the paced rate up to the maximum tracking rate and the associated symptoms. It does not eliminate the post-ectopic pause (the principle of Medtronic Rate Stabilization) and is not a night-time resting rate. Rate Smoothing cannot be programmed On if Sudden Brady Response, which paces at a high rate after a sudden drop in rate, is active.
prog-bbm-009.aRetenir: Rate Smoothing caps the cycle-to-cycle rate change at a percentage of the preceding R-R interval.

prog-bbm-010.question: Regarding Rhythm ID (Boston Scientific ICDs), which statements are correct?
options: It compares the tachycardia EGM with a reference template recorded in sinus rhythm (Vector Timing and Correlation morphology analysis)
In a dual-chamber device, if the ventricular rate exceeds the atrial rate, therapy is delivered without further analysis
It can withhold therapy in the VF zone if the template matches
It relies on beat-by-beat analysis of P-R patterns, without morphology analysis
commentaires: Correct: Rhythm ID compares the tachycardia EGM with an automatically acquired sinus template (Vector Timing and Correlation).
Correct: in a dual-chamber device, V faster than A indicates a ventricular origin and leads directly to therapy.
Incorrect: like all SVT discriminators, Rhythm ID acts only in VT zones, never in the VF zone.
Incorrect: P-R pattern analysis without morphology corresponds to Medtronic PR Logic; Rhythm ID combines morphology and A/V analysis.
prog-bbm-010.explication: Rhythm ID combines morphology analysis (Vector Timing and Correlation, comparing the tachycardia EGM with an automatically acquired sinus rhythm template) with analysis of atrial and ventricular intervals. In a dual-chamber device, a ventricular rate faster than the atrial rate indicates a ventricular origin and leads directly to therapy. Like all SVT discriminators, Rhythm ID acts only in VT zones: it never withholds therapy in the VF zone. P-R pattern analysis without morphology is the logic of Medtronic PR Logic. Boston Scientific's implementation of the 2019 consensus update recommends Rhythm ID in ICDs (Onset/Stability or Rhythm ID in CRT-Ds) and points out that discriminators only apply up to 230 bpm: a VF zone programmed too low therefore deprives fast SVTs of any discrimination. In the RIGHT trial, ICDs using Rhythm ID (VITALITY 2 generation) had more inappropriate therapies than the Medtronic ICDs they were compared with, especially in single-chamber devices and for rhythms < 175 bpm, which argues for high detection rates.
prog-bbm-010.aRetenir: Rhythm ID = morphology correlation with the sinus template + A/V analysis; never inhibits in the VF zone, discrimination limited to 230 bpm.
